newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania repatriation rules seen boosting markets.
newsitem.headline: Romania repatriation rules seen boosting markets.

text.p: New regulations for repatriation of foreign investment in Romania promise to increase capital inflows to the cash-strapped country and boost equities trading, analysts said on Thursday.
But some traders say the new regulations, or norms, discriminate between banks and securities companies, increase red tape and raise the cost of access to capital markets.

"Repatriation rules are normally good news for investors," a western analyst said. "I see rising inflows in the not too distant future from foreign investors whose demand for Romanian equities has been obvious this year."
The central bank approved this week long-awaited regulations on repatriation of profits from greenfield investments, as well as initial investments and capital gains.

Non-residents acting as foreign investors will be given access to the local foreign exchange market to submit spot or forward hard currency orders related to their investments. Up to now, non-residents could place only sell notes.
"The currency market will also reap the fruit of this move, as richer hard currency inflows will help counter traditional dollar hoarding for winter imports," an analyst said.
The new regulations follow a government decree on free repatriation, which set a tax of up to 1.5 percent on each portfolio deal.
To become effective the new norms have yet to be published in the Official Gazette.
Romania's capital market has seen large foreign inflows this year as foreigners, encouraged by the new government's commitment to push ahead stalled market reforms, turned bullish on stocks.
"The norms were needed, as they secure the application of the decree, but brokerage houses are discriminated against and fees for market operations are swelled," a local broker said.

Under the norms, hard currency buying and selling transactions would be recorded in a foreign investor's account and would be handled solely by commercial banks licensed to operate on the Romanian interbank market.
"It will only be more red tape, with portfolio investors having to open one account with the broker and another with a bank and paying commissions to both," the broker added.

"This, as well as the lack of access for securities companies to the primary market for T-bills mean banks are given some sort of monopoly of the capital market," another local broker said. "Securities companies could have been allowed to deal with the banks in the name of their clients."

Under Romanian regulations, access to the primary market for government paper is given only to banks. Foreigners can buy treasury bills through Romanian brokerage houses using inter-company loans and special deposits.
T-bills yields have risen recently, hitting 55 percent on six-month paper this week against 44 a week ago.
Bucharest bourse general manager Stere Farmache said he was more confident of the benefits of the new norms.
"Right after they become effective, we expect a regress in trading as investors check on banking partners. But in the long run, the norms will not be a discouraging factor," he said.
Some local brokers also shared Farmache's views, saying the norms would prevent money laundering and currency crises.
"What (the authorities) want to do is play with the cards close to their chests," a trader said. "They want strict monitoring to keep money laundering reined in and avoid massive outflows," he said.
"It is also a means of keeping an eye on foreign currency trends on the market," he added.
-- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
